name: canary-deployment
context: A release candidate must be exposed to a small, time-limited slice of real production traffic, evaluated against objective criteria, and only then promoted — or automatically rolled back. The slice receiving the change is 'the canary'; the remainder is 'the control'. Because the candidate is exercised by real production inputs rather than a synthetic environment, defects that only appear under production traffic mix are caught while the blast radius is a fraction of the user base. Google frames the cost explicitly: with 100% of requests failing under a global deploy, a 5% canary population turns a 20% error rate into a 1% overall error rate, which is the difference between burning the error budget and preserving it. The release automation must therefore supply three things: a way to deploy to a subset, an evaluation process, and integration of that evaluation into the release decision.
benefits: Blast radius bounded by canary population: a bad release harms a fraction of traffic instead of everyone, preserving the error budget
Evaluation on production-representative conditions: real request mixes, real data volumes and real diurnal traffic expose defects that staging data cannot
Automatic, evidence-based rollback: monitoring business and technical metrics against the control triggers a revert without waiting for a human to notice
Progressive exposure through successive waves — 1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% — each with its own validation window
Capacity testing against real load in a production-like environment, avoiding the need for a separate full-scale capacity-test environment
Safe schema and API evolution via parallel change, keeping both versions runnable while the rollout is in flight
Fine-grained targeting: internal employees first, then one region, brand, tenant or customer cohort
tradeoffs: Multiple versions run in production simultaneously, so version count, state compatibility and debugging complexity all rise
Requires metric selection discipline — metrics must indicate problems and be representative and attributable; before/after comparison is risky when traffic composition shifts
Requires an evaluation pipeline; without automated analysis the canary becomes a manual ritual with no exit criterion
Canary duration must match release velocity: daily deploys cannot afford a week-long canary, and 20 deploys a day need a much shorter one
Running simultaneous canaries contaminates the signal; Google strongly advises only one canary deployment at a time
Not suitable for client-side software the team does not control, because upgrade timing is outside the operator's influence
Temptation to conflate with A/B testing, which corrupts both: regression detection and hypothesis testing have different statistics and timelines
use_cases: Rolling a new ranking model to 1% of traffic and comparing error rates and business metrics against the control before expanding
Facebook-style staged rollout: an employee-only canary with every feature flag on, to catch problems before any external user sees them
Geographic canary — releasing to one region first to expose differences in traffic mix and data residency
Configuration and secret rollouts that carry the same risk as a code change and must be evaluated the same way
Graceful rollout of an Android or iOS client release, where the staged percentage of installed instances rising to 100% bounds backend impact
A database migration deployed alongside the code that reads it, using parallel change so both schema states are valid during the rollout
avoid_when: Traffic is too low for a canary slice to produce statistically meaningful signal within a useful window
There is no way to route a subset of traffic to the candidate version
The team cannot define the metrics that decide promotion, making the canary decorative
Client software is installed on devices the team does not control
Very high release velocity, where the canary bookkeeping would exceed the value of the safety net
component_types: Canary fleet: the instances running the candidate release
Control fleet: the instances running the current release
Traffic router: load balancer weights, proxy configuration, feature flags or DNS-based partitioning that splits traffic
Analysis service: compares canary metrics against the control
Metric pipeline: pre-aggregated, low-latency metrics (request rate, error rate, latency, business KPIs)
Automated rollback controller: reverts routing when the analysis fails
Feature flag service: enables the new behaviour for the canary cohort only
anti_patterns: No automated analysis: the canary advances on vibes rather than on a defined metric threshold
No control group: comparing against yesterday instead of against concurrently running traffic, so traffic-mix changes masquerade as regressions
Concurrent canaries: overlapping experiments that contaminate each other's signal
Canary size chosen for convenience rather than for the statistical power needed to detect the failure being hunted
Conflating A/B testing with canarying: business-metric regression detection and hypothesis testing share infrastructure but must not share interpretation
Canary on an unrepresentative slice — a region or cohort with different data characteristics hides exactly the bugs the canary exists to find
Advancing on wall-clock time alone with no burn-rate or SLO-based exit criterion
design_principles: Partial and time-limited exposure: the candidate runs on a defined slice for a defined window, not indefinitely
Concurrent control: the comparison baseline is the simultaneously running old version, not history
Blast radius proportional to canary population: the impact of a defect scales with the fraction of traffic exposed
Automated, metric-driven decisions: promotion and rollback are policy evaluations, not human judgment calls
Progressive expansion: exposure grows in waves, each wave gated by its own evaluation
One canary at a time: concurrent experiments destroy the attribution the technique depends on
best_practices: Size the canary population and duration against release velocity and against the minimum detectable effect you actually care about
Pick metrics that indicate problems — error rate, latency distributions, and the business metric most tied to the change — not vanity metrics
Ensure canary and control receive representative, equivalently shaped traffic so differences are attributable to the change
Encode promotion and rollback as explicit thresholds wired into the deployment pipeline rather than a manual review step
Use parallel change (expand-and-contract) so schema and API changes keep both versions runnable throughout the rollout
Run one canary at a time per service to keep the signal clean
Roll back first and diagnose afterwards — that ordering is what keeps Mean Time to Recovery low
